data held by public sector bodies. In particular, each Member State should therefore be able to decide whether data is made accessible for re-use, also in terms of the purposes and scope of such access. This Regulation should complement and be without prejudice to more specific obligations on public sector bodies to allow re-use of data laid down in sector-specific Union or national law. Public access to official documents may be considered to be in the public interest. Taking into account the role of public access to official documents and transparency in a democratic society, this Regulation should also be without prejudice to Union or national law on granting access to and disclosing official documents. Access to official documents may in particular be granted in accordance with national law without imposing specific conditions or by imposing specific conditions that are not provided by this Regulation.

(12)

The re-use regime provided for in this Regulation should apply to data the supply of which forms part of the public tasks of the public sector bodies concerned under law or other binding rules in the Member States. In the absence of such rules, the public tasks should be defined in accordance with common administrative practice in the Member States, provided that the scope of the public tasks is transparent and subject to review. The public tasks could be defined generally or on a case-by-case basis for individual public sector bodies. As public undertakings are not covered by the definition of public sector body, the data held by public undertakings should not be covered by this Regulation. Data held by cultural establishments, such as libraries, archives and museums as well as orchestras, operas, ballets and theatres, and by educational establishments should not be covered by this Regulation since the works and other documents they hold are predominantly covered by third party intellectual property rights. Research-performing organisations and research-funding organisations could also be organised as public sector bodies or bodies governed by public law.

This Regulation should apply to such hybrid organisations only in their capacity as research-performing organisations. If a research-performing organisation holds data as a part of a specific public-private association with private sector organisations or other public sector bodies, bodies governed by public law or hybrid research-performing organisations, i.e. organised as either public sector bodies or public undertakings, with the main purpose of pursuing research, those data should also not be covered by this Regulation. Where relevant, Member States should be able to apply this Regulation to public undertakings or private undertakings that exercise public sector duties or provide services of general interest. The exchange of data, purely in pursuit of their public tasks, among public sector bodies in the Union or between public sector bodies in the Union and public sector bodies in third countries or international organisations, as well as the exchange of data between researchers for non-commercial scientific research purposes, should not be subject to the provisions of this Regulation concerning the re-use of certain categories of protected data held by public sector bodies.

(13)

Public sector bodies should comply with competition law when establishing the principles for re-use of data they hold, avoiding the conclusion of agreements which might have as their objective or effect the creation of exclusive rights for the re-use of certain data. Such agreements should be possible only where justified and necessary for the provision of a service or the supply of a product in the general interest. This may be the case where the exclusive use of the data is the only way to maximise the societal benefits of the data in question, for example where there is only one entity (which has specialised in the processing of a specific dataset) capable of providing the service or supplying the product which allows the public sector body to provide a service or supply a product in the general interest. Such arrangements should, however, be concluded in accordance with applicable Union or national law and be subject to regular review based on a market analysis in order to ascertain whether such exclusivity continues to be necessary. In addition, such arrangements should comply with the relevant State aid rules, as appropriate, and should be concluded for a limited duration which should not exceed 12 months. In order to ensure transparency, such exclusive agreements should be published online, in a form that complies with relevant Union law on public procurement. Where an exclusive right to re-use data does not comply with this Regulation, that exclusive right should be invalid.

(14)

Prohibited exclusive agreements and other practices or arrangements pertaining to the re-use of data held by public sector bodies which do not expressly grant exclusive rights but which can reasonably be expected to restrict the availability of data for re-use that have been concluded or were already in place before the date of entry into force of this Regulation should not be renewed after the expiry of their term. In the case of indefinite or longer-term agreements, they should be terminated within 30 months of the date of entry into force of this Regulation.

(15)

This Regulation should lay down conditions for re-use of protected data that apply to public sector bodies designated as competent under national law to grant or refuse access for re-use, and which are without prejudice to rights or obligations concerning access to such data. Those conditions should be non-discriminatory, transparent, proportionate and objectively justified, while not restricting competition, with a specific focus on promoting access to such data by SMEs and start-ups. The conditions for re-use should be designed in a manner promoting scientific research so that, for example, privileging scientific research should, as a rule, be considered to be non-discriminatory. Public sector bodies allowing re-use should have in place the technical means necessary to ensure the protection of rights and interests of third parties and should be empowered to request the necessary information from the re-user. Conditions attached to the re-use of data should be limited to what is necessary to preserve the rights and interests of third parties in the data and the integrity of the information technology and communication systems of the public sector bodies. Public sector bodies should apply conditions which best serve the interests of the re-user without leading to a disproportionate burden on the public sector bodies. Conditions attached to the re-use of data should be designed

, if they are to be the recipients, taking into full account the interests and fundamental rights of the data subject.

(112)

Those derogations should in particular apply to data transfers required and necessary for important reasons of public interest, for example in cases of international data exchange between competition authorities, tax or customs administrations, between financial supervisory authorities, between services competent for social security matters, or for public health, for example in the case of contact tracing for contagious diseases or in order to reduce and/or eliminate doping in sport. A transfer of personal data should also be regarded as lawful where it is necessary to protect an interest which is essential for the data subject's or another person's vital interests, including physical integrity or life, if the data subject is incapable of giving consent. In the absence of an adequacy decision, Union or Member State law may, for important reasons of public interest, expressly set limits to the transfer of specific categories of data to a third country or an international organisation. Member States should notify such provisions to the Commission. Any transfer to an international humanitarian organisation of personal data of a data subject who is physically or legally incapable of giving consent, with a view to accomplishing a task incumbent under the Geneva Conventions or to complying with international humanitarian law applicable in armed conflicts, could be considered to be necessary for an important reason of public interest or because it is in the vital interest of the data subject.

(113)

Transfers which can be qualified as not repetitive and that only concern a limited number of data subjects, could also be possible for the purposes of the compelling legitimate interests pursued by the controller, when those interests are not overridden by the interests or rights and freedoms of the data subject and when the controller has assessed all the circumstances surrounding the data transfer. The controller should give particular consideration to the nature of the personal data, the purpose and duration of the proposed processing operation or operations, as well as the situation in the country of origin, the third country and the country of final destination, and should provide suitable safeguards to protect fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of their personal data. Such transfers should be possible only in residual cases where none of the other grounds for transfer are applicable. For scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes, the legitimate expectations of society for an increase of knowledge should be taken into consideration. The controller should inform the supervisory authority and the data subject about the transfer.

(114)

In any case, where the Commission has taken no decision on the adequate level of data protection in a third country, the controller or processor should make use of solutions that provide data subjects with enforceable and effective rights as regards the processing of their data in the Union once those data have been transferred so that that they will continue to benefit from fundamental rights and safeguards.

(115)

Some third countries adopt laws, regulations and other legal acts which purport to directly regulate the processing activities of natural and legal persons under the jurisdiction of the Member States. This may include judgments of courts or tribunals or decisions of administrative authorities in third countries requiring a controller or processor to transfer or disclose personal data, and which are not based on an international agreement, such as a mutual legal assistance treaty, in force between the requesting third country and the Union or a Member State. The extraterritorial application of those laws, regulations and other legal acts may be in breach of international law and may impede the attainment of the protection of natural persons ensured in the Union by this Regulation. Transfers should only be allowed where the conditions of this Regulation for a transfer to third countries are met. This may be the case, inter alia, where disclosure is necessary for an important ground of public interest recognised in Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject.

(116)

When personal data moves across borders outside the Union it may put at increased risk the ability of natural persons to exercise data protection rights in particular to protect themselves from the unlawful use or disclosure of that information. At the same time, supervisory authorities may find that they are unable to pursue complaints or conduct investigations relating to the activities outside their borders. Their efforts to work together in the cross-border context may also be hampered by insufficient preventative or remedial powers, inconsistent legal regimes, and practical obstacles like resource constraints. Therefore, there is a need to promote closer cooperation among data protection supervisory authorities to help them exchange information and carry out investigations with their international counterparts. For the purposes of developing international cooperation mechanisms to facilitate and provide international mutual assistance for the enforcement of legislation for the protection of personal data, the Commission and the supervisory authorities should exchange information and cooperate in activities related to the exercise of their powers with competent authorities in third countries, based on reciprocity and in accordance with this Regulation.

(117)

The establishment of supervisory authorities in Member States, empowered to perform their tasks and exercise their powers with complete independence, is an essential component of the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of their personal data. Member States should be able to establish more than one supervisory authority, to reflect their constitutional, organisational and administrative structure.

(118)

The independence of supervisory authorities should not mean that the supervisory authorities cannot be subject to control or monitoring mechanisms regarding their financial expenditure or to judicial review.

(119)

Where a Member State establishes several supervisory authorities, it should establish by law mechanisms for ensuring the effective participation of those supervisory authorities in the consistency mechanism. That Member State should in particular designate the supervisory authority which functions as a single contact point for the effective participation of those authorities in the mechanism, to ensure swift and smooth cooperation with other supervisory authorities, the Board and the Commission.

(120)

Each supervisory authority should be provided with the financial and human resources, premises and infrastructure necessary for the effective performance of their tasks, including those related to mutual assistance and cooperation with other supervisory authorities throughout the Union. Each supervisory authority should have a separate, public annual budget, which may be part of the overall state or national budget.

entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.
entity: "MEMBER STATE" | type: "PARTY" | description: A Member State is defined as a sovereign country that is a part of the European Union (EU), thereby subject to its laws and regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation 2016/679). Additionally, Member States play a crucial role in the governance of data intermediation services and data altruism, supporting the responsible sharing and reuse of data for societal benefit, particularly by public sector bodies. They also bear significant responsibilities concerning high-risk AI systems and biometric identification systems, which include reporting their findings related to these areas to the Commission. Each Member State possesses its own market surveillance authorities and has the authority to enforce compliance through administrative fines.

question: Why did the surveillance programmes based on Section 702 FISA and E.O. 12333 fail the requirement of proportionality?
ground_truth: Section 702 FISA does not indicate any limitations on the power it confers to implement surveillance programmes or any guarantees for non-US persons: the FISC authorises programmes, not individual measures, and does not review whether individuals are properly targeted. PPD-28 does not grant data subjects rights actionable in the courts, nor does E.O. 12333, and PPD-28 allows bulk collection without judicial review that is not delimited in a sufficiently clear and precise manner. Those programmes are therefore not limited to what is strictly necessary, as required by the second sentence of Article 52(1) of the Charter.
answer:
The surveillance programs established under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and Executive Order 12333 (E.O. 12333) have faced significant scrutiny concerning their compliance with the principle of proportionality. This principle necessitates that any limitations imposed on rights must be necessary and appropriate, fitting within the context of the legal framework governing surveillance and privacy rights.

### Key Issues with Proportionality

#### Lack of Clear Limitations
One major issue is that neither Section 702 nor E.O. 12333 provides sufficiently precise legal boundaries regarding the scope of surveillance. Section 702 permits the monitoring of non-U.S. citizens located outside the United States for foreign intelligence purposes, but it does not adequately establish limitations on when or how such surveillance can be enacted. Critics note that this lack of clarity allows for potential excessive surveillance practices without strict oversight or accountability.

#### Absence of Judicial Review
The programs outlined in these statutes do not encompass robust mechanisms for judicial oversight. The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) approves general surveillance programs rather than individual surveillance measures. This means that the focus is on broad authorization rather than case-by-case judicial scrutiny, which is pivotal for safeguarding the rights of those being monitored, particularly non-U.S. persons who fall outside the protections that U.S. citizens might receive.

#### Failure to Provide Effective Remedies
The effectiveness of redress mechanisms is crucial under the proportionality principle. Both Section 702 and E.O. 12333 lack provisions that grant data subjects actionable rights against the U.S. government in the courts. This absence of enforceable rights impacts individuals’ ability to contest unlawful surveillance practices leading to the conclusion that the current frameworks do not align with the high standards expected for judicial protection as stipulated by the European Union's Charter of Fundamental Rights.

### Implications of Inadequate Safeguards
As a result of these inadequacies in defining limits, ensuring oversight, and providing for effective remedies, the practical implementation of these surveillance programs arguably does not meet the strict necessity standards that the proportionality principle demands. This is further compounded by the recognition that surveillance based on these frameworks can result in data collection without sufficient justification, thus infringing on the fundamental rights of individuals.

### Conclusion
The failures of the surveillance programs under Section 702 and E.O. 12333 to meet the requirement of proportionality stem from their vague limitations, insufficient judicial oversight, and lack of effective legal redress mechanisms. These shortcomings raise significant concerns about privacy rights and the protection of individuals, particularly non-U.S. citizens, in the realm of international data transfers and surveillance practices. 

In summary, successful implementation of surveillance activities must respect and protect individual rights, which, under the current legislative frameworks, appears notably deficient. Thus, meaningful reforms or alternative measures may be required to align these practices with established human rights standards.

AI systems used for those purposes may lead to discrimination between persons or groups and may perpetuate historical patterns of discrimination, such as that based on racial or ethnic origins, gender, disabilities, age or sexual orientation, or may create new forms of discriminatory impacts. However, AI systems provided for by Union law for the purpose of detecting fraud in the offering of financial services and for prudential purposes to calculate credit institutions’ and insurance undertakings’ capital requirements should not be considered to be high-risk under this Regulation. Moreover, AI systems intended to be used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons for health and life insurance can also have a significant impact on persons’ livelihood and if not duly designed, developed and used, can infringe their fundamental rights and can lead to serious consequences for people’s life and health, including financial exclusion and discrimination. Finally, AI systems used to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to dispatch or establish priority in the dispatching of emergency first response services, including by police, firefighters and medical aid, as well as of emergency healthcare patient triage systems, should also be classified as high-risk since they make decisions in very critical situations for the life and health of persons and their property.

(59)

Given their role and responsibility, actions by law enforcement authorities involving certain uses of AI systems are characterised by a significant degree of power imbalance and may lead to surveillance, arrest or deprivation of a natural person’s liberty as well as other adverse impacts on fundamental rights guaranteed in the Charter. In particular, if the AI system is not trained with high-quality data, does not meet adequate requirements in terms of its performance, its accuracy or robustness, or is not properly designed and tested before being put on the market or otherwise put into service, it may single out people in a discriminatory or otherwise incorrect or unjust manner. Furthermore, the exercise of important procedural fundamental rights, such as the right to an effective remedy and to a fair trial as well as the right of defence and the presumption of innocence, could be hampered, in particular, where such AI systems are not sufficiently transparent, explainable and documented. It is therefore appropriate to classify as high-risk, insofar as their use is permitted under relevant Union

entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.

question: Why does the Privacy Shield Ombudsperson mechanism not satisfy Article 47 of the Charter?
ground_truth: Because it does not provide a cause of action before a body offering guarantees essentially equivalent to those required by Article 47. The Ombudsperson is appointed by the Secretary of State, reports to him and is an integral part of the US State Department, and nothing indicates that dismissal is accompanied by particular guarantees, which undermines its independence from the executive. Nor does anything indicate that the Ombudsperson can adopt decisions binding on the intelligence services, or that any legal safeguards accompany the political commitment to correct violations.
answer:
The Privacy Shield Ombudsperson mechanism has faced scrutiny in relation to Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, which guarantees the right to an effective remedy and a fair trial. The concerns primarily revolve around whether this mechanism provides sufficient judicial protection for individuals whose data privacy rights are violated under the transatlantic data transfer framework established by the Privacy Shield.

### Shortcomings of the Privacy Shield Ombudsperson Mechanism

1. **Lack of Judicial Independence:**
   The Privacy Shield Ombudsperson operates independently from the U.S. Intelligence Community but does not function as a tribunal under EU law. This raises questions about the effectiveness and impartiality of the Ombudsperson's role. Article 47 emphasizes the need for judicial protection that is credible and independent; thus, the Ombudsperson's oversight lacks a formal judicial basis.

2. **Limited Scope of Action:**
   The mechanism primarily addresses complaints regarding the handling of personal data within the context of U.S. surveillance laws. Critics argue that it does not adequately shield individuals from the expansive powers of U.S. surveillance, such as those allowed under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), which permits broad and potentially intrusive data collection.

3. **Insufficient Remedies:**
   Article 47 stipulates that individuals have the right to seek an effective remedy when their rights are infringed. However, the Ombudsperson's ability to provide such remedies has been questioned, as there is a perceived gap in its authority to challenge substantive decisions or engage in effective redress mechanisms. This could result in individuals being unable to obtain satisfactory resolutions for their data protection grievances.

4. **Uncertainty in Legal Protection:**
   The Ombudsperson mechanism lacks clear assurances about the adequacy of protection for personal data, particularly when it is transferred from the EU to the U.S. Without strong guarantees of judicial protection, data subjects may feel disempowered, undermining their rights and the overall efficacy of the data protection framework established by the GDPR.

### Conclusion

Overall, the Privacy Shield Ombudsperson mechanism is seen as inadequate in meeting the standards delineated in Article 47 of the Charter for providing effective judicial protection. There are significant gaps in its structure and enforcement powers that limit its ability to safeguard individuals' data privacy rights effectively. The requirement for stronger oversight and judicial mechanisms remains critical for ensuring that individuals have the means to protect their privacy when their data is processed across borders. 

These shortcomings highlight the ongoing necessity for robust data protection frameworks that can guarantee the rights of data subjects, particularly in light of international data transfers and the varying legal standards that govern them.

entity: "SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY" | type: "PARTY" | description: "The Supervisory Authority is the national body responsible for overseeing compliance with data protection regulations, as referenced in the text."<SEP>The "SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY" is an independent public authority established in each Member State to oversee the enforcement and compliance with data protection laws, particularly under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Its primary role involves monitoring adherence to data protection regulations, ensuring that personal data is handled appropriately, and safeguarding the rights of data subjects.

The SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY is tasked with various functions, including addressing complaints from individuals about personal data processing, conducting investigations, and enforcing compliance through decisions that may be challenged in court. It has the authority to impose administrative fines on entities that violate data protection laws. Additionally, the Supervisory Authority promotes awareness of individual rights related to personal data and facilitates cooperation among Member States in matters concerning investigations and compliance monitoring.

Furthermore, the SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY can approve codes of conduct, issue opinions, and authorize specific data processing activities, thus playing a critical role in protecting fundamental rights associated with personal data. Overall, the Supervisory Authority serves as a key regulatory body responsible for ensuring that organizations operate within the framework of established data protection laws, thereby upholding the rights of citizens regarding their personal information.
entity: "ARTICLE 47" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "Article 47" encompasses significant provisions within the legal framework of the European Union, addressing both judicial rights and compliance requirements related to data protection and AI systems. It guarantees the right to an effective remedy and a fair trial, as articulated in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. This provision ensures that individuals can seek redress in court when their rights, particularly those concerning data protection, are violated. It establishes that EU citizens are entitled to effective judicial protection, which has been invoked in high-profile cases concerning data misuse, exemplified by Mr. Schrems' legal challenges.

In addition to its judicial implications, Article 47 also relates to the regulatory environment surrounding high-risk AI systems. It mandates the creation and documentation of an EU declaration of conformity for these systems, specifying the necessary contents and requirements for compliance. Furthermore, Article 47 outlines the requirements for Binding Corporate Rules (BCR), which facilitate the international transfer of personal data within corporate groups while ensuring adherence to data protection standards.

Overall, Article 47 serves a dual purpose: it provides a foundation for individual rights protection in judicial matters and establishes regulatory requirements aimed at ensuring compliance in the increasingly significant domain of artificial intelligence.
entity: "GDPR" | type: "STATUTE" | description: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a comprehensive regulation in European Union (EU) law focused on data protection and privacy. It is designed to give individuals greater control over their personal data and establishes guidelines for the collection and processing of personal information within the EU. GDPR governs how personal data is handled, sets forth the responsibilities of data controllers and processors, and addresses the transfer of personal data outside the EU.

As a crucial legal framework, GDPR replaced the earlier Directive 95/46, reflecting advancements in technology and changes in societal expectations regarding privacy. It emphasizes the rights of individuals, including their right to access their data, rectify inaccuracies, and request deletion of their information. Overall, the GDPR aims to strengthen the protection of personal data and privacy for individuals within the European Union, making it one of the most significant pieces of legislation in the realm of data protection.

entity: "GDPR" | type: "STATUTE" | description: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a comprehensive regulation in European Union (EU) law focused on data protection and privacy. It is designed to give individuals greater control over their personal data and establishes guidelines for the collection and processing of personal information within the EU. GDPR governs how personal data is handled, sets forth the responsibilities of data controllers and processors, and addresses the transfer of personal data outside the EU.

As a crucial legal framework, GDPR replaced the earlier Directive 95/46, reflecting advancements in technology and changes in societal expectations regarding privacy. It emphasizes the rights of individuals, including their right to access their data, rectify inaccuracies, and request deletion of their information. Overall, the GDPR aims to strengthen the protection of personal data and privacy for individuals within the European Union, making it one of the most significant pieces of legislation in the realm of data protection.

entity: "REGULATION" | type: "STATUTE" | description: "The Regulation sets out the legal framework for the processing and protection of personal data within the European Union."<SEP>REGULATION refers to a comprehensive legal framework established within the European Union to govern the use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and manage the handling, sharing, and processing of data, with a strong emphasis on the protection of individuals' rights. It defines rules and directives that classify AI applications, particularly distinguishing high-risk AI systems and ensuring compliance with fundamental rights.

One key aspect of the REGULATION is its determination of the responsibilities and obligations of providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, as well as those associated with general-purpose AI models. It sets forth guidelines for the classification and assessment of these AI systems, requiring compliance with safety standards and prohibiting manipulative practices, especially in contexts involving biometric data. Additionally, the REGULATION outlines rules to ensure non-discriminatory application and protection of individuals' rights across the Union.

The REGULATION also establishes mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement of AI systems, detailing the functioning of supportive bodies such as advisory forums and scientific panels. It specifies the legal framework for the management of biometric identification systems, including their usage and implications for privacy. The REGULATION encompasses a range of aspects including standardization processes, provisions for interoperability, and the roles and responsibilities of data holders and users of connected products.

Moreover, it aims to facilitate smooth transitions between data processing services, allowing users to efficiently transfer their data and digital assets while ensuring that data access and usage are governed by consent or legitimate interest. It specifies the obligations of data holders and includes provisions for resolving disputes related to data handling, ensuring fairness in contractual arrangements. 

Overall, the REGULATION not only serves to protect individuals' rights—granting them access, rectification, and erasure of their personal data—but also demands consistency in the enforcement of data protection laws across Member States. By establishing these comprehensive guidelines and frameworks, the REGULATION promotes effective data management and enhances trust and security in data processing practices within the European Union.

entity: "COMMISSION" | type: "PARTY" | description: The Commission, specifically referring to the European Commission, is a vital governing body within the European Union responsible for a broad range of functions regarding legislation, compliance, and data protection laws. It plays a central role in proposing new legislation and ensuring adherence to existing EU laws, particularly those related to data protection, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Privacy Shield Decision.

The Commission evaluates the adequacy of data protection levels in third countries, assessing whether their legal frameworks provide equivalent protections for personal data. This role includes the issuance of adequacy decisions that enable lawful data transfers from the EU to third countries, crucial for maintaining privacy standards in international data exchanges.

In addition to its data protection responsibilities, the Commission oversees regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems. It is tasked with ensuring compliance across EU member states by proposing legislation related to both general-purpose and high-risk AI models. This includes the authority to request documentation and assess compliance from AI providers, facilitating the evaluation of safety measures concerning high-risk AI systems.

Furthermore, the Commission adopts delegated acts that establish guidelines and procedural measures for the regulation of AI systems, developing benchmarks for systemic risks and maintaining the coherence of data protection regulations. It also coordinates information exchange among authorities and manages an EU Database to support compliance with the set regulations.

Overall, the Commission is instrumental in shaping not only data protection laws and the regulatory landscape for AI but also in upholding the EU treaties and ensuring transparency and public interest goals are met. Its comprehensive mandate positions it as a pivotal authority in the governance of data and technological advancements within the European Union.

question: Did the Court maintain the effects of the invalidated Privacy Shield Decision to avoid a legal vacuum?
ground_truth: No. The Court declared the Privacy Shield Decision invalid in its entirety, since Article 1 is inseparable from Articles 2 and 6 and the annexes. It held that the annulment of such an adequacy decision is not liable to create a legal vacuum, because Article 49 GDPR details the conditions under which transfers to third countries may take place in the absence of an adequacy decision under Article 45(3) or of appropriate safeguards under Article 46.
answer:
The Court addressed whether to maintain the effects of the invalidated Privacy Shield Decision to prevent a legal vacuum, which could arise from the annulment of an adequacy decision. According to the ruling, while the annulment of the Privacy Shield Decision might suggest the potential for a legal vacuum, the Court determined that such a vacuum would not be created. It highlighted that the provisions of Article 49 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) already outline the conditions necessary for transferring personal data to third countries in the absence of an adequacy decision, thus avoiding a scenario where there are no applicable legal frameworks in place.

The ruling also indicated that even though the Privacy Shield framework was deemed invalid, organizations could still ensure compliance with EU data protection laws through alternative legal instruments, such as Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs). These mechanisms would provide the necessary safeguards for the transfer of personal data, ensuring that individuals' rights are adequately protected, and that data processors and controllers adhere to the regulatory requirements set by the European Union.

Moreover, the Court made it clear that when individuals lodge complaints regarding the transfer of their personal data, the supervisory authorities have a duty to assess if such transfers meet the GDPR standards, regardless of the status of the Privacy Shield Decision. This emphasizes that the fundamental rights of individuals under EU law must remain safeguarded.

Overall, the Court ruled that the invalidity of the Privacy Shield Decision does not lead to a legal vacuum and that alternative provisions under existing regulations still offer adequate protection for personal data transfers between the EU and third countries, particularly the United States.

In the light of the factors mentioned by the Commission in the Privacy Shield Decision and the referring court’s findings in the main proceedings, the referring court harbours doubts as to whether US law in fact ensures the adequate level of protection required under Article 45 of the GDPR, read in the light of the fundamental rights guaranteed in Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter. As far as concerns effective judicial protection, it adds that the introduction of a Privacy Shield Ombudsperson cannot, in its view, remedy those deficiencies since an ombudsperson cannot be regarded as a tribunal within the meaning of Article 47 of the Charter.

In particular, the question whether the finding in the Privacy Shield Decision that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection is binding is relevant for the purposes of assessing both the obligations, set out in paragraphs 141 and 142 above, of the controller and recipient of personal data transferred to a third country pursuant to the standard data protection clauses in the annex to the SCC Decision and also any obligations to which the supervisory authority may be subject to suspend or prohibit such a transfer.

As to whether the Privacy Shield Decision has binding effects, Article 1(1) of that decision provides that, for the purposes of Article 45(1) of the GDPR, ‘the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the [European] Union to organisations in the United States under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield’.
